article.overview: A spectrometer calibration source is a reference device carried on a lunar mission so that an on-board spectrometer can check its own response during the mission. It either emits a known signal (for example, alpha particles or X-rays from a sealed radioactive source, or light from a lamp) or presents a reference surface of known properties (for example, a metal or rock target, or a reflectance panel) that the instrument views on command. Measurements of that reference are compared with the values expected for it, so drifts in detector gain, energy scale, or illumination can be tracked and corrected before the instrument's measurements of the lunar surface are interpreted. No single calibration source design is standard for lunar missions. The examples in this article are not interchangeable: one is a Mars instrument, one is a lunar rover instrument whose lander did not operate on the surface, and one is a lunar rover instrument that did operate. Only the last has a documented lunar surface operation in the sources reviewed here.
article.description: Spectrometers on planetary surfaces must be calibrated, and their performance can change with time. Detectors age, temperatures change, contamination accumulates, and optical or mechanical alignments shift after launch and landing. A calibration source gives the instrument a repeatable reference inside the same environment as its science measurements. Two broad forms are used. Emitting sources include sealed radioactive sources (commonly curium-244 in planetary alpha-particle X-ray spectrometers) that emit particles and X-rays with known energies, and lamps or other emitters that can serve the same role for optical spectrometers. Passive reference targets are plates or slabs with known composition or reflectance that are viewed by the instrument, usually with the Sun or an internal light source providing illumination. Common materials include metals (stainless steel, aluminium, titanium, copper, nickel) and well-characterised rock, and reflectance panels are used for optical spectrometers. In either form the reference is usually protected from dust, because lunar dust is abrasive and electrostatically charged and can coat optical windows, sources and calibration plates.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a calibration source is to make surface measurements interpretable. Specific applications include checking the energy or wavelength scale of an X-ray, gamma-ray or optical spectrometer; tracking changes in detector sensitivity over the mission; verifying the intensity of a known emission line or reflectance value; providing a reference for comparing a flight instrument with its laboratory twin; and identifying instrument degradation caused by dust, temperature or radiation. For lunar surface spectroscopy these checks matter because mineralogical and elemental interpretations depend on the instrument's absolute response. Reflectance measurements in particular need a reference target whose properties are independently known.
article.operating_principle: For an emitting source, the principle is that the source produces radiation of known energy or spectrum. The instrument records the response, and the recorded peaks or spectral features are compared with the known values. Any offset or change in shape indicates a calibration change that can be corrected in software or in the interpretation of the data. For a passive reference target, the instrument views the target under known or measured illumination, and the measured radiance or reflectance is compared with the expected value for that target. Where the instrument has an internal calibration unit, it can switch between viewing the surface (detection mode) and viewing the reference (calibration mode). The accuracy of the correction depends on how well the reference is characterised, how stable it remains over time, and whether it is kept free of dust.
article.scientific_importance: Accurate spectroscopy is central to lunar science. Elemental composition, mineral identification, surface maturity (space weathering) and reflectance mapping all depend on the instrument's absolute response. Without a calibration reference, a spectrometer can produce data that look precise but carry unknown systematic errors. Calibration sources therefore support the scientific value of the spectrometer itself, not only its engineering health. The lunar spectroscopy literature also uses lunar surface sites as reflectance references, but those site-based references are different from on-board calibration sources and are not discussed further in this article.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size, source activity or power requirement for a spectrometer calibration source. The values below describe specific instruments and are tied to their sources. Where a value was not found in the sources reviewed, it is recorded as not publicly specified. The examples span very different designs and must not be compared as equivalent.

examples.name: Mars Pathfinder Alpha Proton X-ray Spectrometer (APXS)
examples.type: Planetary instrument (Mars); flown and operated on Mars; not a lunar instrument
examples.mass_source: NASA Planetary Data System instrument description, dataset mpfr-m-apxs-2-edr-v1.0 (Mars Pathfinder rover)
examples.calibration_sources: Nine curium-244 alpha-particle sources and three detectors for each of three types of particles (PDS description). Source activity not stated on the cited page.
examples.calibration_method: Flight sources and sensor head cross-calibrated against laboratory sources before launch; a laboratory unit identical to the flight instrument is used in ongoing calibration tests; alpha and proton modes to be recalibrated at Martian pressures (PDS description).
examples.on_board_passive_calibration_target: Not described on the cited PDS page.
examples.power: Not stated on the cited PDS page.
examples.detectors: X-ray: Si-PIN photodiode in a hermetically sealed package with a beryllium window. Alpha: silicon, 35 µm thick, designed to stop 6.5 MeV alpha particles. Proton: silicon, thick enough to stop protons up to 6 MeV.
examples.qualification: Figures are for the Mars Pathfinder APXS as described in the PDS dataset and must not be transferred to the Curiosity APXS.

examples.name: Mars Science Laboratory (Curiosity) APXS calibration target
examples.type: Planetary instrument (Mars); flown and operating on Mars; not a lunar instrument
examples.status: Flown; operating on the surface of Mars
examples.calibration_target: The APXS shares a calibration target area with the Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) at the end of the robotic arm (NASA JPL, PIA15284). A search excerpt describes the APXS target as a slab of well-characterised basaltic rock surrounded by nickel plate, used periodically to check performance; this excerpt was not verified against the full primary page and is provisional.
examples.source_activity: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.power: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.qualification: Pathfinder APXS values (Example 0) are not assumed for this instrument.

examples.name: Chandrayaan-2 Pragyan rover APXS (not operated on the Moon)
examples.type: Lunar rover instrument; pre-flight design described in published literature
examples.status: Not operated on the lunar surface. The Pragyan rover was carried by the Vikram lander, which lost contact during descent in September 2019; sources reviewed state the rover never left the lander. Current mission status should be checked against ISRO official communications.
examples.calibration_target_plate: Aluminium plate carrying four metallic targets (stainless steel, aluminium, titanium, copper), chosen to cover a wide X-ray energy range; allows tracking of changes in alpha flux, alpha energy and X-ray flux over time. The plate also protects the detector and sources from lunar dust (pre-flight arXiv paper, arXiv:1910.09232, search excerpt).
examples.source_isotope_and_activity: Not confirmed in the sources reviewed. The Mars curium-244 design is not assumed to apply.
examples.dimensions: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.power: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.
examples.qualification: No measured values from this instrument are presented.

examples.name: Chang'e-3 Visible and Near-Infrared Imaging Spectrometer (VNIS), Yutu rover
examples.type: Lunar rover spectrometer with an integrated calibration unit; flown and operated on the Moon
examples.status: Operated on the lunar surface after the Chang'e-3 landing in Mare Imbrium; mounted at the front of the Yutu rover (instrument abstract).
examples.calibration_unit: Calibration unit with dust-proofing functionality (instrument abstract). A search excerpt states the unit can be moved for surface detection, in-flight calibration and dust protection, and that the VNIS includes a white calibration panel; the instrument works in calibration mode when aimed at the calibration target. These details come from search excerpts and need full-paper verification.
examples.in_flight_calibration: Abstract states in-flight calibration satisfied the requirements for scientific detection.
examples.power: Not stated in the sources reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The examples span very different scales. The Pathfinder APXS is a compact sensor head with sealed sources and a documented mass of 570 g. The Curiosity APXS shares a calibration target area on the robotic arm, with dimensions not verified here. The Pragyan APXS design is described only at the level of its calibration plate. The VNIS is a rover-mounted spectrometer with an integrated calibration unit. Dimensions cannot be meaningfully compared without instrument-specific data, which are not available here for most examples.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Documented mass is available for one example only: the Mars Pathfinder APXS at 570 g (PDS description). Masses for the Curiosity APXS, Pragyan APXS calibration plate and VNIS calibration unit are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Mass for a new calibration source would depend on the sealed-source or target design, shielding, mounting and the host instrument.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power is not stated for any example in the sources reviewed. Power for a new calibration source would depend on whether it is passive (a target) or active (a lamp or heated reference), and on the host instrument's thermal and detector needs.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar calibration source must survive launch, cruise, landing and the lunar surface environment. The Moon has no substantial atmosphere, so temperature swings are large, radiation levels are high, and micrometeoroid impacts are possible. Dust is a particular concern because it can cover optical windows, obscure a calibration plate or contaminate a radioactive source window, so protective covers, shrouds or movable units are common design features. Sealed radioactive sources require handling and regulatory controls during integration and launch; these are not described in detail in the sources reviewed. Passive reference targets must keep stable properties, because dust deposition or thermal cycling can change them over time and their condition should be monitored or periodically checked.
article.limitations: A calibration source corrects only the instrument's response to the source or target it observes; it does not guarantee accuracy for every surface material or every energy. Source decay, dust contamination and thermal changes can reduce the stability of the reference and need to be modelled or checked periodically. Passive reference targets depend on illumination and viewing geometry and require consistent measurement conditions. Several design details in this article come from search excerpts and abstracts and should be confirmed against full primary papers before engineering use.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A spectrometer calibration source would normally be part of a larger instrument or rover payload rather than a separately deployed device, so its transportation requirements depend on the host system. Two of the three lunar-relevant examples are rover-mounted (Pragyan APXS, VNIS); the Curiosity APXS is mounted on a robotic arm. No example establishes a specific lunar lander or rover interface for a new calibration source.
transportation_process: Integrate the spectrometer and its calibration source or target into the rover or lander payload on Earth; sealed radioactive sources require special handling and documented approval for integration.
Launch the spacecraft and perform cruise operations, during which calibration references should be protected.
Deliver the rover or payload to the lunar surface.
Deploy the rover or position the instrument so that its calibration target or source can be viewed or used.
Operate the instrument in both detection and calibration modes, and monitor the reference over time.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Deployment depends on the host system. The VNIS was mounted at the front of the Yutu rover. The Pragyan APXS was designed for a rover that was to roll out from its lander by ramp; that rollout did not occur. The Curiosity APXS is positioned by the robotic arm.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Chang'e-3 VNIS operated from the Yutu rover on the lunar surface. The Pragyan APXS was carried by the Chandrayaan-2 Vikram lander, which was lost during descent in September 2019. The Mars APXS instruments illustrate sealed-source and target calibration on another planet.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: The compatibility of a future calibration source with a particular lunar lander or rover would need to be assessed from its mass, dimensions, mounting interface, sealed-source handling requirements, calibration-target exposure, power and data interfaces. It should not be assigned to a specific lander until those requirements have been compared with verified spacecraft specifications. No compatibility with a named lander is asserted in this article.

article.historical_significance: Calibration references have been used on planetary surface instruments for decades. Mars APXS instruments have used sealed sources (Pathfinder) and calibration targets (Curiosity) for in-situ elemental analysis. On the Moon, the Chang'e-3 VNIS provided in-situ spectral reflectance data from the Yutu rover, and its data have been used in reflectance analyses of the landing site, which a 2018 study proposed as a calibration site. The Chandrayaan-2 Pragyan APXS design shows a dust-protected calibration plate for a lunar rover, but the instrument did not operate on the surface.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Source activity, calibration target materials, mass and power are not publicly specified for the Pragyan APXS and the VNIS in the sources reviewed. The Curiosity calibration target description comes from a search excerpt and has not been verified against the full NASA primary page. The Pragyan source isotope is not confirmed and the curium-244 design is not assumed for it. The VNIS calibration unit details, including the white panel and mode switching, come from search excerpts and need full-paper verification. The Pathfinder APXS mass (570 g) and nine-source count are not assumed for any other instrument. Only the VNIS among the examples has documented lunar surface operation in the sources reviewed. Full-resolution image downloads were not checked.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Mars Pathfinder APXS figures (570 g; nine curium-244 sources) come from the PDS dataset mpfr-m-apxs-2-edr-v1.0 and are not transferred to the Curiosity APXS.
The Curiosity APXS basaltic-rock and nickel calibration target description comes from a search excerpt, not the full primary page; treat as provisional.

Pragyan APXS calibration plate details come from a pre-flight arXiv paper seen through search excerpts; the source isotope and activity are unconfirmed. The rover did not operate on the lunar surface; mission status is based on 2019 news and encyclopedia reporting and should be checked against ISRO official communications.
VNIS calibration unit details (white panel, calibration mode) come from search excerpts; spectral ranges and lunar operation come from the IOP abstract. Mass and power are not stated.
Only one image was included, verified to return HTTP 200. No additional images were verified and none are placed.
Full-resolution image downloads were not checked.
